item.title: You Know How to Eat Well, So Why Can't You?
item.description:
Diet

You Know How to Eat Well, So Why Can't You?

Psychology explains why eating mindfully can be difficult—and what you can do.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Internal conflicts and mixed societal messages make mindful eating harder than it seems.
  • The fantasy that weight loss brings happiness fuels unhealthy eating behaviors.
  • Occasional "junk food" can fit into a healthy eating pattern without shame.

For years, eating disorder specialists have been telling us that we need to eat “mindfully,” that we need to “listen to our bodies,” and that we need to sort out emotional causes of overeating from genuine hunger. My PT colleague Mitchell B. Liester recently wrote a post about research showing that healthy eating can improve depression in some cases as much as an antidepressant. But despite the panoply of available therapies to address these issues and find a way to be comfortable in our bodies, minds, and lives, these sensible directions can be difficult to follow.

Although I no longer work specifically with eating disorders, I have found that many of the clients I work with in psychotherapy have a troubled relationship with food and with their bodies. That’s not really surprising to me. Most of the people I know outside of my work have similar difficulties.

You know what to do. What makes it so hard to do it?

Which brings me to the question: what makes it so hard to follow the healthy suggestions of so many psychotherapists, nutritionists, and, increasingly these days, psychiatrists? And my answer is: the psychological underpinnings of food and eating issues are widespread and complex.

But they can be dealt with.

The universal fantasy about weight loss

One factor is an almost universal fantasy, as Mary Anne Cohen, author of Ozempic for Smarties: A Psychotherapist Tells the Straight Skinny, writes in a recent post, “that weight loss will finally make you whole, happy, and more lovable.”

For another, we have so many different voices in our psyches that it’s hard to sort out what is “really” coming from us. These opinions, coming from family, cultural, medical, and general interactions with others, cloud our ability to trust ourselves.

You can eat well and also enjoy so-called "junk food"

Cecily* was a perfect example. She had struggled with an eating disorder in her teens, but now, as a 27-year-old, she was making a conscious effort to eat well. Most days she had a healthy breakfast of yogurt and fruit every morning, lunch of a salad and soup or a sandwich of fresh chicken with extra lettuce, and a protein, starch, and two vegetables for dinner. She drank plenty of water and had an occasional snack of dried fruit and nuts.

But there were days when she grabbed a donut off the office coffee cart for breakfast and had a bag of chips and a candy bar for lunch. And on far too many nights, dinner was a slice of pizza or some other fast food.

From her psychotherapist when she was an adolescent, she had learned that fast foods and packaged snacks like potato chips appeal to an evolutionarily based craving for salt and fat, which helped our ancestors survive. “But they also are easier and cheaper than cooking for myself,” she said. She also knew that her binges were often triggered by emotional issues. “I’ve learned to address those problems head on,” she said. “And I haven’t binged for ten years.”

Still, Cecily, like many of us, often felt ashamed that she could not control her cravings. She worried that she was “just lazy,” and she assumed other people had the same criticism of her.

Your internal map

“My therapist told me I had to learn to listen to myself,” she said. “When I want chips or a candy bar, I’m listening to myself. And when I think I’m too heavy, I’m listening to myself. But those thoughts are supposed to be wrong. I’m confused. I’m probably remembering wrong, or maybe I’m just not remembering at all. Maybe she said something else that I’ve just forgotten.”

I believe that we each have an internal “map” that guides us as we move through life. That map starts small, with just the self that interacts with our family. As we grow and mature, the map expands to take in the rest of the world with which we interact—friends, teachers, religious leaders, and eventually the world around us as well.

Internal conflict: Choosing a direction over and over again

From very early, we have to deal with internal conflict about what direction to take, which road to follow on our map. For a small child, that conflict may start as a disagreement between what they want and what their parents want, but before too long it becomes an internal question of whether they want to please their parents or please themselves.

I told Cecily that I thought she probably was remembering correctly, but that what she was describing now was one of the things that makes listening to yourself difficult: internal conflict. “You want to eat healthily,” I said, “but sometimes you want to eat something that’s not quite so healthy. That’s internal conflict—an internal argument about which direction to go on your personal map.”

Cecily said, “That’s so interesting. I know I eat pretty well. I exercise regularly, sleep well, and have a terrific guy in my life who tells me he loves how I look.” But recently several people had told her that she looked like she was losing weight, and that had triggered her self-doubt.

“Are you losing weight?” I asked.

“I don’t think so. I don’t weigh myself, but my clothes still fit the same.”

“So if these people hadn’t said anything, you wouldn’t be concerned?” I asked.

She nodded. “Even though you sometimes grab chips or candy or fast foods?” I asked.

“Well, I don’t love that. I try to eat well, but sometimes you have to cut yourself some slack,” she said.

You're not alone: Other people have their own food and eating issues

The people who commented on her weight probably had their own food and weight issues—something it’s always important to keep in mind when considering someone else’s opinion about your body. Their comments triggered some of Cecily’s own concerns and highlighted that she was straying from the direction of “healthy eating” outlined on her personal map.

As we talked, though, Cecily realized that her map included side-trips to “fun” eating. “A slice of pizza isn’t completely unhealthy,” she said. “Maybe a candy bar or bag of chips is; but on my map, getting off the main road is perfectly OK and maybe even worthwhile, as long as I don’t stay on that path too long.”

My PT colleague Gia Marson would probably agree. In an informative post about healthy, mindful eating, she points out that “diets rarely create lasting, healthy change.”

This information can be added to your personal eating map. It will not end your internal conflict, but the additional choices can provide more information that allows you to choose the path on your personal map that makes the most sense for you.

*Names and identifying info changed to protect privacy.

item.title: How the Emotionally Intelligent Manage Mistakes With the 3 R's
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

How the Emotionally Intelligent Manage Mistakes With the 3 R's

An emotionally intelligent person often does three things after making an error.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Emotionally intelligent people often do the "three R's" after making a big mistake.
  • They take responsibility without excuses, justifications, or attempts to shift the blame.
  • They often reflect deeply on the mistake and then begin to repair by making permanent changes.

Emotionally intelligent people are self-aware, which means they quickly take responsibility for a mistake. Typically, they do not wait until they get caught. If an error is brought to their attention, they do not immediately deflect and shift the blame by playing the victim. They reflect—and this reflection is not superficial, it is deep. They think about what led them to make this mistake, how it impacted the people around them, and how to repair things and make them right.

1. Responsibility

Taking responsibility is not something an EI person takes lightly. They are truly remorseful about their transgression and offer a sincere apology free from excuses, justifications, or a victim stance. They own the misstep fully and completely. Authentically owning it requires a hearty self-esteem and a desire to be a better person.

For example, Sally was extremely busy at work. She remained completely focused throughout the day and even canceled lunch with Anne, her close friend and co-worker. After work, she realized that she had forgotten that Anne’s grandbaby, Ava, had surgery that morning. Kicking herself, she thinks about how that probably hurt Anne’s feelings and possibly made her day harder than it already was. She puts herself in Anne’s shoes and wonders if Anne felt terrified and alone all day.

That evening, she calls Anne, who does not pick up. Sally recognizes that Anne is probably exhausted from worry and is not surprised when she does not answer. Sally leaves a heartfelt apology for Anne.

“I messed up, Anne, and I am so sorry. I hope today went well for Ava and your family. I apologize for being so self-absorbed. I am thinking about you. Call me if you need to talk. See you tomorrow.”

Sally’s apology is free from excuses, minimizations, and an attempt to shift the blame or play the victim. It is very emotionally intelligent. Conversely a non-EI apology usually sounds like this, “Hi Anne, I was buried in work today, so I’m sorry I didn’t get a break to ask you about Ava. I am completely swamped with zero help from anybody. I do not know how long I can do this… You know my work is critical and needs all my attention, so next time, remind me.”

Not only is this apology packed with justifications for the mistake, but Sally plays the victim and shifts the blame to make it Anne’s fault for not reminding her.

2. Reflection

Following the identification of a mistake, an EI individual does not just apologize and move on like it is no big deal, nor do they become hysterical and play the victim to garner sympathy in place of providing it to the people that they negatively affected. Instead, they think about it for a while. Despite their ability to remain regulated and to continue forging ahead, their misstep is continually on their mind.

They think about what led them to this error in judgment. Was it their ego, pride, or insecurities that are to blame, or did they have a selfish moment? Whatever their flaw, they self-analyze until they can pinpoint it. Once they do, they gain insight about a part of themselves that needs attention. Their desire to be a better person pushes them to find a way to address the underlying cause. They now know themselves better and understand what issues set the stage for their mistake. This allows them to gain insight and permanently change and grow. Rarely do they make this type of mistake again because they have evolved in an important way.

3. Reparation

Making things right is one of the most critical aspects of how an EI person manages a big mistake. They do not just say “whatever” and move on. They recognize how it impacted everyone involved, and they empathize, but it does not end there. They find a way to communicate how their blunder impacted those around them, so these folks know that, despite the situation, they are cared about. They may also offer a kind gesture like a pretty plant or a specialty coffee. Not only do they say that they are sorry, but they go out of their way to prove that they are.

In many instances, they will make pragmatic changes to prevent the transgression from happening again. For example, they formally give their staff a half-day a month for a family emergency, or they put reminders in their calendar about their friends and family.

It may seem like EI people go through an awful lot of stress because they are responsible, reflect, and spend time repairing, but to an EI person it is worth it. At the end of the day, they recognize that they have grown in important ways while also ensuring that their relationships with those around them are stronger than ever. You can find more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist, Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, at Work, and in Life.
